Start with the shape of the game
Cribbage uses a standard 52-card deck. Each player is dealt six cards, discards two to the crib, and then the starter card is cut from the deck.
Clubs, diamonds, hearts, and spades each have thirteen ranks. Suit matters for flushes and his nobs. Most fifteens, pairs, and runs care about rank or value instead.
Aces count as 1. Number cards keep their number. Jacks, queens, and kings each count as 10. The rank still matters for pairs and runs.
Every distinct combination totaling 15 scores 2 points. A hand can contain several fifteens, and each one is counted separately.
Two cards with the same rank score 2 points. Three of a kind contains three separate pairs, and four of a kind contains six.
Three consecutive ranks score 3 points, four score 4, and so on. Suits may be mixed. Duplicate ranks can create double, double-double, or triple runs.

After the discard, the non-dealer cuts the deck and the starter card joins both hands and the crib. It can create new fifteens, pairs, runs, a flush, or his nobs. A jack as the starter also pegs 2 for the dealer, called his heels.
If your hand contains a jack that matches the starter card's suit, score one point for his nobs. The jack does not need to match the starter's rank.
Both players discard two cards to the dealer's crib. The dealer counts the crib after counting their own hand, so dealer discards are both an opportunity and a risk.
Players move pegs along a board with 120 holes plus a final game hole. The first player to reach 121 wins, so a safe point now can matter more than a perfect-looking hand later.
How many points does a single combination totaling 15 score?
Each distinct combination totaling 15 scores 2 points.
What value does a queen contribute to a fifteen?
Jacks, queens, and kings each have a cribbage value of 10, while their ranks stay distinct for pairs and runs.
The crib belongs to the dealer. Both players contribute two cards to it.
A jack matching the starter's suit
His nobs is one point for a jack matching the starter card's suit.
How many cards does each player receive before discarding?
The standard deal gives each player six cards. Each player then discards two to the crib.
Can a run use mixed suits?
Runs use consecutive ranks. The suits can be mixed.
How many points does a pair score?
Two cards of the same rank make one pair worth 2 points.
What is the usual winning hole on a cribbage board?
Cribbage is normally a race to 121 points.
What happens after the two players discard?
The non-dealer cuts the deck and the starter card is placed face up before pegging begins.
Which cards all count as 10 for fifteens?
All cards above 9 count as their rank
Tens, jacks, queens, and kings each contribute 10 to a fifteen.
A 5 with a ten-value card is one fifteen. The ace, the 4, and the same ten-value card make another. When a hand has several small cards, check combinations systematically so none are missed.
This example has two separate pairs for 4 points. Three cards of one rank create three pairs, not one three-of-a-kind score.
Three in sequence scores 3, four scores 4, and five scores 5. Duplicate ranks can create multiple runs, so sort the cards before counting.
Four cards of the same suit score 4 in a hand. If the starter also matches, the hand flush is 5. The crib has a stricter flush rule: all five cards must match.
The jack is watching the cut
A jack matching the starter card's suit scores one point. In a real count, keep the jack in view until you know the cut.
A pair can multiply a run
The 4-5-6 sequence appears twice because there are two 4s. That is 6 points for the two runs, plus 2 for the pair. Count any fifteens separately.
Use the same order every time. Count fifteens first, then pairs, runs, flushes, and his nobs. Add the starter-driven bonuses as you go.
The hand count is not the whole game
During pegging, points come from making 15, pairs, runs, 31, go, and the last card. The same cards can score differently in this phase because order matters.
The 5 with the 10 is a clear fifteen, and the 2, 3, and 10-value card make another 15. There is no pair or four-card flush.
Three 7s create three separate pairs for 6 points. They are not a run, and no jack is present.
The four cards from 4 through 7 form a run of four. The suits are mixed, so this is not a flush, and there is no jack to watch.
Four of the five cards are diamonds, so a hand holding those four has a four-card flush worth 4, or 5 if the starter is a diamond too. Nothing here adds to fifteen and no rank repeats.
The hand contains a heart jack. If the starter is a heart, that jack becomes his nobs for one point.
The 3-4-5-6 shape is a four-card run, and the second 3 lets it form twice. That double run of four is 8 points before the pair is counted.
Two combinations reach fifteen: the 6 with the 9, and the 5 with the queen. No rank repeats and nothing runs three deep, so 4 points of fifteens is the whole count.
Only the two 10s share a rank, so there is exactly one pair. Queen and king are also worth 10 toward a fifteen, but rank is what pairs, and 10-queen-king skips the jack so there is no run.

The first decision after the deal
Each player receives six cards and discards exactly two. The four cards you keep are your hand. Both players' discards make up the dealer's crib.
The same hand has two different jobs
The dealer scores the crib later, so a dealer can accept a slightly weaker hand when the discarded pair is likely to make a useful crib. The pone tries to starve it.
A 5 pairs with every ten-value card for a fifteen and connects with small cards. As pone, discarding a 5 is often risky unless your hand improves dramatically.
A pair is already worth 2. Break it only when the replacement creates a much stronger mix of fifteens, runs, or a flush, and account for what the crib will receive.
The cards talk to each other
Keep cards that make several shapes
A 4, 5, and 6 can make runs and fifteens. The more combinations a card participates in, the more expensive it is to throw away.
When you are pone, look at the cards you are giving the dealer. Avoid giving a pair, a 5, or two cards that immediately make 15 together when a similar hand score is available.
The starter is random, so do not build a discard around one miracle card. Favor a hand that already scores and has several useful cuts.
During the hand count, the same starter joins your hand and the crib. During pegging, the discarded cards are gone, so use the information to estimate what remains.
You are pone. Choose 2 cards to discard.

Keep 2-3-4-5 for a run of four. Trading the 5 away would be worse: it is the single most useful card in the deck, and as pone every card you throw lands in the dealer's crib. The 10 and king neither pair nor make fifteen together, so they are the cheapest pair to give up.
As pone, judge a discard by what it gives the dealer, not only by what it costs you.
You are the dealer. Choose 2 cards to discard.

Keep 5-5-10-Q. Each 5 makes fifteen with the 10 and again with the queen, so that is four fifteens for 8, plus 2 for the pair: 10 points before the cut. The 6 and 7 are connected ranks that may build a run in your own crib. They total 13, so they do not score a fifteen by themselves.
As dealer, evaluate the hand and the crib together.
You are pone. A flush is available. Choose 2 cards.

Keeping the four hearts preserves a four-card flush and gives the starter a chance to extend it. The off-suit 4 and 9 do not create a stronger structure together, and neither is an appealing gift as a pair.
Four cards of one suit are already a meaningful hand feature.
You are the dealer. Where does the pair do the most work?

Keeping the 7s with the 3 and 5 is the best hand that holds the pair, 6 points before the cut. Throwing the 7s keeps 3-4-5-10 for 5, a run plus the 5-10 fifteen, and puts a pair in your own crib, where it is worth about two points more than the 4 and 10 would be.
A dealer's own crib is a safe home for a pair that does not fit the hand.
You are pone. Which two cards starve the crib best?
Keep 5-6-9-K for two fifteens: 6 with 9, and 5 with the king. Throwing the 2 and the 8 gives the dealer two cards that neither pair nor reach fifteen together, and it keeps the 5 out of the crib.
For the pone, crib defense is part of your score.
You are the dealer. Keep the double run alive.
The two 4s with 5 and 6 make a double run of three. The 9 and queen are isolated from that shape and do not form a useful pair or fifteen with each other.
Duplicate ranks can multiply a run, so sort before discarding.
You are the dealer with a high-card-heavy deal.

Keep 10-10-J-Q. The second 10 lets 10-jack-queen form twice, a double run of three for 6, plus 2 for the pair. Dropping the king breaks nothing, because 10-jack-queen-king would only be a single run of four, and the 4 connects to nothing here.
Ten-value cards make few fifteens, but they still pair and run by rank.
You are the dealer and the board is tight. Choose two.

The 3-4-5 block plus a ten-value card is the most connected hand here: a run of three and the 5-10 fifteen, with many helpful cuts. The 7 and 8 are not a loss either, because they already make fifteen in your own crib.
The board can make a safe, countable hand the best hand.

All five cards share a suit. Keeping four gives a 4-point hand flush; only a matching starter makes it 5.
Keeping the four suited cards would give a 4-point hand flush. A matching starter would make it 5; a crib flush always needs all five.
The ranks build a run worth %lld points. Suits never matter for a run, and aces stay low.
Matching ranks are worth %lld points here. Three of a rank is three separate pairs, not one score.
Combinations totaling fifteen are worth %lld points here. Court cards count 10 and the ace counts 1.
The pattern includes a jack. It scores nobs only if kept and matched by the starter's suit.
Cribbage is a race to 121 points. You score by making combinations in your hand and crib, then by playing cards in order during pegging. The first player to reach the finish wins.
A fifteen is any combination of cards totaling 15, worth 2 points.
Use a standard 52-card deck. Aces are low and count as 1. Number cards keep their values, while jacks, queens, and kings count as 10 for fifteens.
Each player receives six cards and discards two to the dealer's crib. The non-dealer cuts the starter card, which joins both hands and the crib for scoring.
The dealer wants a strong crib. The pone tries to starve it.
Score every combination of 15, then pairs, runs, and flushes. Add one for his nobs when a jack matches the starter's suit. The same starter card can create several bonuses at once.
Count in the same order every time so your points do not disappear.
After the starter is cut, players alternate playing one card while keeping the running total at or below 31. Score for 15, pairs, runs, 31, go, and the last card.
Say the running total out loud. It is the center of every pegging decision.
That is the whole loop: choose a discard, peg carefully, count every combination, and keep an eye on the board. The drills teach each skill one room at a time, five minutes at a stretch.
A 5 connects with every ten-value card for a fifteen and is one of the most valuable cards to keep. Discard the card that creates the fewest combinations with the rest of the hand.
As dealer, you count both your hand and the crib. When two keeps have equal value, favor the discard with more crib potential. The pone does not score your crib.
Avoid points in your own crib
As pone, the crib belongs to the dealer. A discard that is fine for your own hand may still cost you if the two cards pair, make fifteen together, or include a 5.
A pair guarantees 2 points before the cut. Do not break it casually just to chase a speculative run unless the complete hand shape makes the trade worthwhile.
A run has room to grow
A 4-5-6 run is already 3 points. Cards that extend it or create fifteens are valuable, while an isolated queen offers fewer connections here.
A four-card flush is real value
Four matching suits score 4 in the hand, and a matching starter would make 5. Keep the suited block when the other cards do not offer a clearly stronger structure.
The 5 already makes a fifteen with the 10 and king. It can also connect with small ranks into runs, so it is usually a keeper in a close choice.
Count the board, not just the cards
When either player is close to 121, a conservative discard and safe pegging line can beat a higher theoretical hand. Cribbage is a race, not only a counting puzzle.
How many cards does each player discard to the crib?
Each player discards exactly two cards. The dealer's crib then contains four cards before the starter is cut.
What is a king worth toward fifteen?
Every face card counts as 10 for fifteens, even though its rank stays jack, queen, or king for pairs and runs.
What does the first player to 121 do?
Standard cribbage is a race to 121. A player who reaches the finish first wins immediately.
Who usually cuts for the starter card?
The non-dealer cuts the deck after both players have discarded.
Can an ace be high in a run?
Aces are low in cribbage. A, 2, 3 is a run, but Q, K, A is not.
What is the safest way to count a complicated hand?
Use a fixed order and check every combination
Count the cut card last and ignore it
A repeatable count order, such as fifteens, pairs, runs, flush, and nobs, prevents omissions and double counting.
2-3-4 is a run of three. No rank repeats and only two cards share a suit, so the run is the shape on the table. Two fifteens hide behind it for a full count of 7.
Each 5 makes fifteen with the 10 and again with the jack. Four fifteens is 8 points, before the pair of 5s adds 2 more.
Four hearts make a four-card hand flush worth 4, or 5 if the starter is a heart too.
Three 9s contain three separate pairs for 6 points. There is no consecutive sequence, though each 9 does make fifteen with the 6.
6-7-8-9 is a run of four. The king sits apart from that sequence, and the two fifteens, 6 with 9 and 7 with 8, are counted separately.
The heart jack becomes his nobs if the starter is a heart. Nothing here runs three deep and only two cards share a suit, so the jack is the shape to watch.
You are pone. Choose two cards without feeding the crib.
Keep 3-4-5-10, which is rich in runs and fifteens. The 9 and king are the least connected cards, and they do not make 15 together.
Pone should protect the crib as well as build a hand.
You are the dealer with a pair and a run. Choose two.
Keep the pair of 4s and the 5-6 connection. The pair is guaranteed value, while 10 and queen are the least integrated cards in this deal.
Dealer decisions weigh both the hand and the crib.
You are pone and four cards share a suit. Protect the flush.

Keeping the four clubs is 4 for the flush plus 2 for the 2-4-9 fifteen, and a club cut makes the flush 5. The 7 and king are off-suit, do not pair, and do not reach fifteen together, so they cost the dealer's crib very little.
A four-card flush is already a real source of points.
You are pone near the finish. Favor the hand you can count safely.

Keep 2-3-4 with the 9: the run scores 3 and 2-4-9 makes fifteen. Holding the 9 rather than the 10 matters on the discard side, because 8 and 10 give the dealer nothing, while 8 and 9 hand over a run start.
The board can make a dependable point more valuable than a risky maximum.
During pegging, what do you announce when the running total reaches 15?
A pegging total of exactly 15 scores 2 points.
What happens when a play brings the running total to 31?
The player scores 2 and the count resets
Reaching exactly 31 scores 2 points, then the running count resets for the remaining cards.
What is a go in pegging?
A player cannot play without exceeding 31
When you cannot play without going over 31, you say go. The opponent may continue if they can.
A play makes a pair during pegging. How many points is that?
A pair in the pegging sequence is worth 2 points, just like a pair in the hand.
Who scores the last-card point in a pegging sequence that does not reach 31?
The player who played the last card
The player who plays the final card before the count resets scores 1 for last card.
When should you think about the board position?
Before choosing a discard and during pegging
Never, the highest hand always wins
Cribbage is a race. Board position should shape discards, pegging risk, and whether you chase points or safety.
A 5 connects with every ten-value card and is a dangerous crib gift. Keep it unless the hand improvement from discarding it is overwhelming.
Break it for a thin possibility?
A pair is 2 points before the starter. Keep it unless the alternative creates a much stronger, clearly countable hand.
A one-point lead alone does not decide your strategy. Consider the actual scores, who counts first, and likely pegging. Choose the line that best serves the race.
The 4 makes 31 for 2 points. Playing the 8 would exceed 31, so the legal safe play is the 4.
A rule allowing an opponent to claim missed points

Muggins is an optional rule, agreed before play. Under ACC rules, after a player releases the peg or forfeits a score, the opponent may claim missed play, hand or crib points. Missed heels (the starter jack), penalties, muggins points and backward-pegging losses are excluded.
What is required for a five-card flush in the crib?
All four crib cards and the starter match
A crib flush requires all four crib cards plus the starter to be the same suit.
A duplicate rank inside a run
A duplicate rank gives the consecutive sequence two ways to be formed, doubling the run's points.
Aces are low in cribbage, so A-2-3 is a run. The ace does not wrap around from king.
The pone's hand, then the dealer's hand and crib
The dealer's crib, then the pone
The player with the higher score
The pone counts first, then the dealer counts their hand and finally the crib. The order affects who can win before the other player counts.
The count goes from %lld to %lld. That is not 15 or 31, the %@ does not match the card played just before it, and the last cards form no run of three, so you score nothing.
The count goes from %lld to %lld. You score %@, %lld in all. A pegging run counts the last cards played in any order, and a pair only counts against the card played just before.
How many cards are in the crib before the starter is cut?
Each player contributes two cards, so the dealer's crib has four cards before the starter joins it.
What does a 5 combine with most readily?
A 5 plus any 10, jack, queen, or king is a fifteen worth 2 points.
Does a run need matching suits?
A run is about consecutive ranks. The suits may be mixed.
Only the four crib cards match
The crib's flush rule is stricter than a hand flush: all five cards, including the starter, must match suit.
Which card can be his nobs?
A jack matching the starter suit
Any card matching the starter rank
His nobs is one point for a jack whose suit matches the starter.
Three ways to make the same run
Three copies of a rank inside a run create three distinct ways to form that sequence.
The pone counts first, then the dealer counts their hand and the crib. The order can decide a close game.
What is an ace's value in a fifteen?
An ace counts as 1 and is low in runs.
8-9-10-jack is a run of four. Rank order is what builds a run, so the jack sits directly above the 10 even though both are worth 10 toward a fifteen.
Three 7s contain three separate pairs for 6 points, not a single three-of-a-kind score. Nothing here reaches fifteen and there is no jack.
Four spades create a four-card hand flush worth 4, or 5 if the starter is a spade too.
2-3-4-5 is a run of four, and the second 2 lets it form twice. That double run of four is 8 points before the pair of 2s adds 2 more.
The 5 makes fifteen with the 10 and again with the queen, and 2-5-8 makes a third. Three fifteens is 6 points, with no repeated rank and no sequence.
Four of a rank contain six separate pairs for 12 points. The king is not consecutive with the 7s and only two cards share a suit.
You are pone. Keep the broadest scoring hand.

Keep 3-4-5-6: a run of four for 4, plus the 4-5-6 fifteen for 2. Swapping the 6 for the 10 looks similar but drops the run to three cards. The two ten-value cards neither pair nor make fifteen together, so they are the safest thing to hand the dealer.
Count combinations, not just the prettiest sequence.
You are the dealer. A pair sits inside a run.
Keep 6-6-7-8. The second 6 gives 6-7-8 two ways to form, a double run of three for 6, plus 2 for the pair and 2 for the 7-8 fifteen: 10 points before the cut. The 2 and the king touch none of that.
A pair inside a run is worth far more than a pair on its own.
You are pone with four diamonds. Choose two cards.
The four diamonds preserve a hand flush and give the cut a chance to make five. The off-suit cards are not a pair and do not form a fifteen together.
As pone, do not give away a pair or a clean fifteen when you have another path.
You are pone and the board is close. Choose the easy hand to count.
The 2-3-4 block has a clear run path and the 10 helps a 5 if the cut arrives. The 9 and queen are the least integrated cards.
Reliable points are often worth more than a fragile ceiling.
Playing the 5 makes 31 for 2 points. The ten-value card would go over, so the legal choice is clear.
Throw one to avoid a bad crib?
A pair scores 2 before the cut. Breaking it is a major trade, not a default defensive move.
The dealer is one point from 121
Should you gift a 5 to the crib?
The dealer is already at a finish line. If your hand can stay competitive without discarding the 5, protect the crib and make the opponent work for the win.
Say the score out loud and peg 2 points before the next player acts. Verbalizing the total keeps the sequence honest.
A jack matching the starter's suit scores one point. Keep a separate nobs check in your count routine.
You are pone. The bigger hand is the wrong hand. Choose two.

Keeping A-A-6-8 counts 6 and A-A-5-8 counts 4, so the bigger hand is two points better. It is still the wrong choice: the cards it throws are a 5 and a queen, which already make fifteen in the crib you do not own. Throw the 6 and the queen instead and hand over nothing that scores by itself.
As pone, subtract what the crib gains before you compare two hands.
You are the dealer, choosing between a pair and a flush.

The four hearts count 6 before the cut: 4 for the flush and 2 for 6-9. The pair of 5s also builds your own crib. This choice has the best combined hand-and-crib average under the drill's random-discard model.
When dealer, a pair can be a feature of the crib rather than the hand.
You are pone with four ten-value cards. Choose two.

Keep 5-10-J-Q. The 5 makes fifteen with each of the three ten-value cards, and 10-jack-queen is a run of three, so the hand counts 9 before the cut, with a jack that can add his nobs. The king and the 4 neither pair nor make fifteen together in the dealer's crib.
A high card count can be worse than a lower count if the crib swings the race.
You are pone. Keep the hand with more useful cuts.

Breaking the pair of 8s costs a guaranteed 2, but 3-4-5 with one 8 already scores 5: the run is 3 and 3-4-8 makes fifteen. The low block also improves on far more cuts, and an 8 with a king is a quiet gift to the dealer.
Useful cuts are a distribution, not one favorite card.
You are the dealer. Choose the discard that works twice.

Keep 2-3-10-J: 2-3-10 and 2-3-jack are two fifteens, and the jack can still add his nobs. For this deal, throwing 7-8 gives the best combined average in the drill's random-discard model. They already make fifteen in your crib.
Discard choices can set up the crib before the cut is turned.
You are pone and your lead is safe. Choose two.

Keep 4-5-6 with one 10: the run is 3, 4-5-6 makes fifteen, and 5 with the 10 makes another, for 7 points. Breaking the pair of 10s costs 2, but the 10 and queen make neither a pair nor a fifteen in the dealer's crib, and the 4-5-6 block is the shape most cuts improve.
Know whose crib you are feeding before evaluating any discard.
The opponent is at 120 and counts next. What matters most?
Whether you can win before they count
Cribbage is a race. If the opponent can reach 121 while counting first, ordinary hand value may not matter.
During pegging, which card is often safest to lead from a small connected hand?
A card that avoids giving an immediate 15 or pair
Pegging defense depends on the running total and your opponent's likely replies. There is no universal safe rank, but avoiding obvious 15s and pairs is a strong start.
You have a choice between pegging 31 now or saving a card for last. What should decide it?
Board position, opponent cards, and the reset
A 31 is 2 points, but saving a card can deny the opponent a go or earn last card. Use the board and the unseen cards, not a single rule.
Why track discarded ranks during the hand?
To predict which runs and pairs remain possible
Known discards reduce the live copies of ranks and help you judge both hand potential and pegging danger.
What is the most common counting error in a double run?
Counting a pair as a flush
A duplicate rank creates multiple ways to form the same run. Count each distinct run, then count fifteens and pairs separately.
When should you choose a lower expected hand over a higher one?
When the board and crib swing make it the better race decision
The correct decision maximizes your chance to win, not the number printed by a hand calculator in isolation.
The second 4 gives 4-5-6 two ways to form, a double run of three worth 6. Add 2 for the pair and 6 for three fifteens, two of them 4-5-6 and one the 5 with the 10, and the hand counts 14.
Every 5 makes fifteen with the 10 and again with the jack, and the three 5s together also total fifteen. Seven fifteens is 14 points, before 6 more for the three pairs.
Four hearts make a hand flush worth 4, or 5 if the starter is a heart too. No rank repeats and there is no jack, so the suit is the only one of these three shapes on the table.
6-7-8-9-10 is a five-card run worth 5, regardless of the mixed suits. It also hides two fifteens, 6 with 9 and 7 with 8, for a full count of 9.
Four 2s contain six separate pairs for 12. The 2s and the 10 reach 12, 14, 16, and 18 but never fifteen, so the duplicate rank is the entire count.
The 5 makes fifteen with the 10 and again with the jack, for 4 points. Nothing repeats a rank, and 4-5 never reaches a third consecutive card.
Two 3s and two 4s let 3-4-5 form four different ways, 12 points of runs. Add 4 for the two pairs and 4 for the two fifteens and the hand counts 20.
Ace through 5 is a five-card run for 5 points, and the five cards together total exactly fifteen for 2 more. Aces are low, so the run starts at the ace.

Which scoring pattern or potential can you spot? No starter is designated.
Look for any combination of cards whose values add to 15. A ten-value card pairs with a five, while smaller cards can make several combinations.
Two cards of the same rank score a pair. Three of a rank makes three pairs, and four makes six pairs.
Three or more consecutive ranks score a run. Duplicate ranks can multiply the run through pairs.
Keeping four matching cards gives a hand flush. A matching starter extends it to five. This pattern exercise does not designate a starter.
A jack in the hand can become his nobs when the cut matches its suit. It is easy to miss because the cut decides it.
